title: BlitzScale: Fast and Live Large Model Autoscaling with O(1) Host Caching
technique: Network-multicast parameter loading over GPU compute network (O(1) host caching) plus layer-level live autoscaling (ZigZag scheduling) so scaled instances serve before parameters fully load

optimized_metrics.evidence: An MaaS system has two design objectives: maximizing goodput—the number of requests that meet the service level objective (SLO), and minimizing instances provisioned to each model to improve hardware utilization.

An MaaS system has two design objectives: maximizing goodput—the number of requests that meet the service level objective (SLO), and minimizing instances provisioned to each model to improve hardware utilization.
Autoscaling speed is critical in minimizing SLO violations because the queued requests are not served until the instances are scaled.
We set TTFT and TBT SLO based on inference speed of different models following prior works
There are three metrics to minimize for the generation: (1) the scale time, (2) the plan generation time, and (3) the interference with serving workloads.

headline_claim.text: BlitzScale achieves up to 94 % lower tail latency reductions compared to state-of-the-art autoscaling system (ServerlessLLM), and it reduces the GPU time used for serving by 49 % when compared with serving systems that do not support autoscaling like DistServe and vLLM with the same service-level-agreement.

metric_definitions.definition_quote: Prefill is evaluated with the time-to-first-token (TTFT) while decode is evaluated using time-between-tokens (TBT).

SLO defines the tolerable end-to-end latency measured from the time a request is sent to the system to the time the inference response is returned. Thus, the latency includes the queueing delays waiting for the scaled instance to be ready for inference.
metric_definitions.notes: latency incl. queueing and scale-up wait; applied to TTFT and TBT separately

metric_definitions.definition_quote: We follow the traditional 5 × SLO [81] since all our workloads (chat and code generation) are latency-sensitive. Specifically, if a request's end-to-end (TTFT or TBT) latency is exceeds 5 × the average latency, it violates the SLO.
metric_definitions.notes: 5x average latency; per-request TTFT or TBT; motivation section instead uses absolute TTFT/TBT SLOs (450 ms/150 ms Llama3-8B; 1250 ms/200 ms Qwen2.5-72B)

metric_definitions.definition_quote: goodput—the number of requests that meet the service level objective (SLO)
metric_definitions.notes: count of SLO-meeting requests; not reported as a plotted metric

slo_spec: Motivation (§3.1): TTFT 450 ms and TBT 150 ms for Llama3-8B; TTFT 1250 ms and TBT 200 ms for Qwen2.5-72B (TP4), based on inference speed following DistServe. Evaluation (§6): 5x average latency (traditional 5x SLO); also users expect <1 s response for chatbots, requiring <500 ms scale time
load_regime: trace replay (BurstGPT, Azure Code, Azure Conversation) scaled to cluster capacity
tradeoff_acknowledged: vs fully over-provisioned DistServe (full) BlitzScale has same SLO attainment but uses far less GPU time; DistServe (half) provisioned for half peak has poorest performance; live scale yields more benefit on TTFT than TBT
hardware: Cluster A: 4 servers x 8 A800 80GB (NVLink 1.6 Tbps); Cluster B: 2 servers x 8 A100 80GB (PCIe 256 Gbps)
workloads: BurstGPT, Azure Code, Azure Conversation traces
